newsitem.title: USA: Education fails to prevent lower back injuries.
newsitem.headline: Education fails to prevent lower back injuries.

text.p: Educational programmes designed to prevent job-related lower back injuries apparently do not work, according to a five-year study involving thousands of postal workers at two U.S. mail processing facilities.

Published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, the study is important because 70 to 80 percent of all adults experience lower back pain at some time in their lives. The condition also accounts for 15 to 25 percent of the injuries covered by workers' compensation and is a major problem for businesses.

Researchers used physical therapists to give roughly half the 4,000 employees three hours of training, plus follow-up briefings on how to properly lift heavy objects and avoid injuries. The remaining workers received no training.

The research team, led by Lawren H. Daltroy of the Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, found that the subsequent injury rate of 2.1 percent per year per worker was essentially the same as it had been before the special training.

When 360 injured workers returned to work, half of them who had received previous training received more; the other half who had received no training previously were briefed on preventing back problems.
It still made no difference, the Daltroy team found.

"The education programme did not reduce the rate of low back injury, the median cost per injury, the time off from work per injury" or the risk of having a repeat injury after returning to work, the researchers concluded.
The only difference: workers who got the training were more knowledgeable about how to prevent such injuries.
"Back-education programmes may still have a place in reducing back injury and disability," the group concluded, "but they appear to be ineffective when undertaken alone."
